title: Rajab and Sha'ban
hook: the months of preparation before Ramadan

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabi' al-Awwal, the month tradition gives for the Prophet's birth and death, kept with a mawlid by some and like any other month by others. Your line: his month. What did your page about his life tell you? Today, the two months before the big one. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven.

'A'ishah lived close enough to notice his habits, and one of the things she noticed was the shape of his fasting through the year. In Sahih al-Bukhari she says, in paraphrase: I never saw him fast a complete month except Ramadan, and I never saw him fast more in any month than in Sha'ban. So the month right before Ramadan wasn't a pause, a last chance to eat before the fast. It was the month he fasted most of all, outside Ramadan itself. Today: Rajab and Sha'ban, the road up to the door.
screen: `WHAT 'A'ISHAH NOTICED.` → `MOST OF ALL IN SHA'BAN.` → `THE ROAD UP TO THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, Rajab. You met it a few days ago: the sacred month that stands on its own, between Jumada and Sha'ban. So the run-up to Ramadan begins inside sacred time, with the verse's instruction still ringing: wrong not yourselves in them. Second, Sha'ban, and why. In a report kept by al-Nasa'i, Usamah ibn Zayd asks the Prophet the obvious question: I don't see you fast in any month the way you fast in Sha'ban. His answer, in paraphrase: it's a month people neglect, between Rajab and Ramadan. And it's a month in which deeds are lifted up to the Lord of the worlds, and I love for my deeds to be lifted up while I'm fasting. A month people neglect. Squeezed between a sacred month and the month of the fast, it's easy to skip. He didn't. Third, catching up. 'A'ishah says in al-Bukhari that when she owed fasts from the last Ramadan, she would make them up in Sha'ban. So Sha'ban is also the month for settling accounts before the next Ramadan arrives. Fourth, the middle of Sha'ban. Some communities keep the night in the middle of the month with extra prayer, remembering the dead and asking forgiveness. Other scholars hold that the reports about that night are weak, and they don't set it apart. Both sides speak from the reports as they read them. Put together, the shape is a runner's warmup. Nobody wakes up and races. You stretch. You test the legs. Rajab and Sha'ban are the stretching: a little fasting, a little extra prayer, the old debts cleared, so that when Ramadan opens, the body and the habits are already moving.
screen: `RAJAB: SACRED TIME FIRST.` · `SHA'BAN: THE MONTH PEOPLE NEGLECT.` · `CATCHING UP ON OLD FASTS.` · `A WARMUP, NOT A PAUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: prepare one habit. Settle, and breathe. Think about the weeks ahead, whether or not you'll fast in Ramadan. Pick one small habit you'd like to be steady by then. Waking a little earlier. Reading a page a day. Drinking water before coffee. A few minutes of quiet. Just one. Now picture doing it tomorrow, at the exact time and place. Then the day after. A warmup is small on purpose. If you pray, you can ask for help keeping it. The bell holds the time.
Rajab and Sha'ban. The two months before Ramadan: a sacred month, then the month the Prophet fasted most outside Ramadan, a time people neglect. Today's word.
Your line: getting ready. Today, do the habit you picked once, even for one minute, so it has already started. Tomorrow, Ramadan: planning. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Muslims add voluntary fasts in Sha'ban, following 'A'ishah's report in al-Bukhari that the Prophet fasted most in that month outside Ramadan, and make up missed Ramadan fasts before the next one begins; some communities also keep the night of the middle of Sha'ban with extra prayer, while others don't set it apart.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rajab and Sha'ban are just the months you pass through on the way to Ramadan.
what it means: a sacred month and then a month of extra fasting, a warmup that gets the body and habits moving before Ramadan.
what a scholar hears: 'A'ishah's report in al-Bukhari, Usamah's question in al-Nasa'i about deeds being lifted up, and the old debate over the night of mid-Sha'ban.
